lines: A scientist came back from holiday to find mould on his germs.
It was September 1928, and his name was Alexander Fleming.
Before leaving, he had spread germs called staphylococci on culture plates.
He left them on a bench in a corner of his lab.
On one plate, a mould had moved in.
Right around the mould, the germs were destroyed.
Farther away, they grew as normal.
You see, it's like the dry ring under an umbrella in the rain.
Something was keeping the germs away.
The mould was making its own germ killer.
For months, Fleming called it mould juice.
In 1929, he presented it to fellow scientists.
His talk got no particular attention.
Years later, Ernst Chain and Howard Florey's team in Oxford turned it into a drug.
By D-Day in 1944, there was enough penicillin to treat all the wounded Allied troops.
When Chain heard Fleming was coming to visit, he was stunned.
He had thought Fleming was dead.
In 1945, all three shared the Nobel Prize.

claims.claim: On 3 September 1928 Fleming returned from a holiday and found one culture contaminated with a fungus.
Before his holiday he inoculated staphylococci on culture plates and left them on a bench in a corner of his laboratory.
Colonies immediately around the fungus were destroyed, while colonies farther away were normal.
For some months he called it mould juice, then named it penicillin in 1929.
He presented the discovery on 13 February 1929 to the Medical Research Club; the talk received no particular attention.
Ernst Chain and Howard Florey's Oxford team developed penicillin; by D-Day in 1944 enough had been produced to treat all the wounded Allied troops.
When Chain heard Fleming was coming he remarked that he thought Fleming was dead.
Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain.
